stories.title: The Pheasant and the Feast
stories.fortuneLine: Do not bless the nest until you have tasted the floor, and do not call the feeding kindness until the solstice table is set.
stories.body:
A pheasant, torn by wolves at the wood’s edge, dragged itself into a farmyard and fell among the hens.

The farmer’s wife bound its wing with clean linen. The children fed it cracked corn from their palms, and named it as if naming were a kind of keeping.

Winter came. The bird grew sleek, then heavy, then too fat to lift itself over the fence. It no longer dreamed of the sky. The yard was warm. The grain was sure. The wolves were only a story told to the dogs.

One evening, from the kitchen window, it heard the farmer say, “He’ll look beautiful on the table.”

The pheasant understood then that it had been saved for the feast, not from it.

When the first thaw came, it tried the air and found its wings were only ornaments. It stood in the yard, listening to the knives being sharpened on the back step, and wondered whether the wolves had ever been the crueler thing.

stories.title: The Rabbit’s Nest
stories.fortuneLine: Do not bless the nest until you have tasted the floor, and do not call the feeding kindness until the solstice table is set.
stories.body:
A rabbit fled a hawk into a hole it had never seen.

The tunnel was warm. A mole-voice said, “Come further. You are welcome.” The rabbit went down, and down, and the hawk’s shadow passed from the mouth of the earth.

It was kind in the dark. There was food that did not run. There were soft walls that seemed to remember the shape of a body.

On the third day the rabbit looked up and found the roof was stone. It looked down and found the floor was bones — small and stacked, each the size of a rabbit who had also been welcome.

The mole-voice, closer now, said, “It’s where you’re safe. It’s where you’ve always been.”

The rabbit did not answer. The tunnel did not open.
